paragraphs: A frozen splash is one of those props that has to be modelled rather than simulated when the deadline is real. This one holds 39,909 polygons of liquid caught mid-throw, with the crown, the trailing droplets and the thin sheet between them all built as geometry you can light directly instead of waiting on a fluid solve.

Two texture maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 carry the surface. StemCell certification means the PBR setup is standardised, so the same splash reads correctly under a studio HDRI in an offline render and inside a real-time engine without anyone rebuilding the shader. UVs are non-overlapping, which matters the moment you want to paint a tint or a product colour onto the liquid.

The page also carries a viscous oil splash built on the same idea, so you can pick between water-thin and heavy without hunting for a second product. It has sold 280 times since 2016, mostly into beverage and cosmetics work where a splash sells the pour better than the bottle does.

Grass is where scatter systems either sell a shot or ruin it. This centipede grass clump is built at 659,020 polygons and 1,203,889 vertices, which is heavy for a single tuft and exactly right as a source object: you scatter a handful of instances, let the renderer deduplicate the mesh, and the lawn holds up at ground level instead of turning to mush half a metre from camera.

Six texture maps at 1500 x 1500 and 1024 x 1024 cover the blades, including the translucency that makes warm season grass read as living rather than plastic when the sun is behind it. UVs are non-overlapping, so a colour shift from spring green to late-summer straw is a texture edit and not a remodel.

A second, more generic warm season variant sits on the same page for scenes where the species does not need naming. Sold 229 times since 2015, usually into architectural exteriors and golf-course or stadium work where the lawn is most of the frame.

An anatomically shaped male skull at 8,954 polygons, which is the sweet spot for a prop that needs to be recognisable from any angle without eating the budget of a medical scene. The suture lines, the orbital rims and the zygomatic arches are in the mesh, so the silhouette survives close-ups; everything finer comes from four maps at 2048 x 2048 and 1024 x 1024.

CheckMate Pro certification means it arrives at real-world scale with clean quads and tris, named materials and no stray geometry, which matters when a skull has to be positioned inside a head rig or dropped into an educational scene that a client will inspect frame by frame.

The page gathers the whole skull family: the female counterpart, both anatomy-model versions, and two decorative sculpts for horror and prop work. Same subject, different intent, sitting together instead of scattered across five near-identical listings. Sold 228 times since 2016, into medical illustration, education and games.

562 polygons, built as quads only, and that is the whole point. A cherry leaf is a component part: you need hundreds of them on a branch and thousands in an orchard, so every polygon spent here is multiplied by the scatter count. This one keeps the blade shape and the serrated edge in geometry and pushes the rest into texture.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the veining, the waxy top surface and the paler underside, which is what separates a convincing leaf from a green card. Non-overlapping UVs mean you can age the leaf toward autumn with a single map swap instead of building a second asset.

Two relatives share the page: a cherry with its leaf attached for close product shots, and a more detailed realistic tree leaf. At $9 it is the cheapest useful building block in the botanical range, and it has sold 226 times since 2017.

A five-panel trucker cap at 10,023 polygons, with the mesh back, the foam front panel and the curved brim built as separate shapes so the cap can sit on a head rig or hang on a hook without deforming into a blob. The seam lines and the plastic snap closure are modelled, because those are the two details a viewer uses to tell a real cap from a generic hat.

CheckMate Pro certification covers the boring things that cost time later: real-world scale, clean topology and materials named the way a lighting artist expects. Drop it into a character scene and it is the right size for a human head on the first try.

The page carries the whole colourway run built on this shape: dark green, forest green and an olive cap alongside this grey one. Same block, different fabric, which is why they are one product rather than four pages that compete with each other. Sold 213 times since 2021, mostly into character and apparel visualisation.

A gerbera is mostly ray florets, and there are a lot of them: 86,447 polygons go into the disc and the two rows of petals, which is what lets the bloom hold its shape when the camera comes close enough to see the pollen. The stem and leaves are modelled to match, so the flower can stand in a vase or lie on a table without cheating the geometry.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the petal gradient, the fine hairs on the stem and the darker centre. CheckMate Pro certification and non-overlapping UVs mean a colour change is a texture job, and that is precisely how the rest of this page came to exist.

Eight versions sit together here: pink, red and yellow blooms, two arrangements already placed in a vase, and a couple of alternative bloom shapes. Pick the colour the set needs instead of buying the same flower twice. Sold 200 times since 2017, into interiors, packaging and floral advertising.

133,790 polygons for the exterior of a Model S P100D, built to hold up in a moving shot: the panel gaps, the flush door handles, the frunk line and the wheel detail are where the budget went, because those are the parts an audience reads as correct or wrong in half a second.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover paint, glass, rubber and the interior surfaces that show through the greenhouse. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology, so the car parks correctly against a street scene without a scale hunt, and the wheels sit where a rig expects to find them.

Three more versions share the page: the 2015 body, and rigged builds of both model years for anyone who needs the wheels turning and the doors opening. This is an editorial licence asset, so it belongs in film, simulation, games and design work rather than in advertising for the brand. Sold 200 times since 2017.

A modern slab phone at 15,329 polygons, which is enough for the chamfered rail, the camera bump and the rounded display corners to survive a macro shot, and light enough that a dozen of them in a conference scene cost nothing. The screen is a separate surface, so swapping in a UI render or an emissive map takes seconds.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 handle glass, metal and the matte back. StemCell certification standardises the PBR materials, which is the difference between a phone that looks right in a game engine and one that turns into a mirror the moment it leaves the renderer it was authored in.

Ten versions live on this page: the plain black, gold and golden bodies, plus the iPhone 11 run in purple, green, black, red, yellow and white. The branded ones carry editorial terms; the unbranded phone does not, and that is the one that usually ends up in commercial work. Sold 196 times since 2020.

An offshore turbine at 106,481 polygons, built generic on purpose: no manufacturer badge, no licensing question, just the monopile, transition piece, nacelle and three blades in the proportions the industry actually uses. That makes it safe for client-facing energy work where a recognisable brand would be a problem.

Three maps at 4096 x 4096 cover the painted steel, the anti-corrosion yellow of the access platform and the subtle weathering that keeps a white tower from looking like plastic against a grey sea. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which matters more here than almost anywhere: a turbine is a size argument, and a wrong one is visible next to a service vessel.
A second tower version sits on the same page for wider farm layouts. Sold 196 times since 2017, into renewable energy presentations, infrastructure animation and simulation work.

A full-size pickup at 287,722 polygons with a simple interior, which is a deliberate trade: the exterior carries the detail an audience looks at, and the cab holds shape without the seat stitching and dashboard switchgear nobody sees through tinted glass. For traffic, parking lots and background action that is exactly the right split.

Eleven maps at 4096 x 4096 cover paint, chrome, rubber, glass and the bed liner. CheckMate Pro certification means clean topology, real-world scale and materials named predictably, so the truck merges into a city scene without a cleanup pass.

It is a generic body, not a licensed one, which is the reason it keeps selling: no brand approval, no editorial restriction, nothing to negotiate before it appears in a commercial render. Sold 196 times since 2019, into architectural visualisation, games and simulation.

A classic jointed teddy bear, the kind with a slightly overlarge head and stubby limbs, because that is the proportion people read as a toy rather than as a small animal. The shape is built to hold up in close-up product work and to survive being posed by hand in a child's bedroom set.

This page is really about the rigging options. Alongside the plain model there are four rigged builds: a general rigged version and dedicated ones for Maya, Cinema 4D and Modo. Pick the one your scene already speaks, instead of importing a rig that needs an hour of repair before the arms bend correctly.

CheckMate Pro certification covers scale, topology and naming, so the bear sits correctly on a bed or in a pair of hands without a scale hunt. Sold 194 times since 2016, into interiors, advertising and character work.

An unbranded thin-and-light laptop at 30,842 polygons, modelled with the lid open and the hinge, port cutouts and keycaps built as geometry rather than painted on. That matters when the camera comes over the shoulder of a character: a flat keyboard texture is the first thing that gives a desk scene away.

Twelve maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover the aluminium body, the display bezel and the keys. The screen is its own surface, so dropping in a UI mockup or an emissive render is a one-click job. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology.

The page collects the closely related builds: a slim design laptop, and two Samsung ATIV Book 9 15-inch versions for when the shot needs a specific machine. The Samsung ones carry editorial terms; the generic laptop does not. Sold 175 times since 2015, into office interiors, product visualisation and UI presentation.

A hinged shell opened just enough to show the pearl, built at 4,484 polygons in quads only. Low as that sounds, a shell is a smooth object: the ribs and the lip carry the read, and subdivision handles the rest if a jewellery shot needs it.

Five maps at 4096 x 4096 do the heavy lifting, including the nacre on the inner surface, which is the whole reason anyone buys this model. StemCell certification means the PBR materials are standardised, so the iridescence behaves the same way in a real-time engine as it does under a studio HDRI, instead of flattening to grey plastic.

A second version with the pearl sitting differently in the shell shares the page, useful when the composition needs the highlight in another spot. Sold 171 times since 2018, into jewellery advertising, cosmetics packaging and beach scenes.

A standard 10.4 mm jewel case at 13,194 polygons, with the tray, the hub teeth and the hinge pins modelled properly. Those are the parts that fail when a case is faked with boxes: the teeth catch light in a way that tells a viewer instantly whether they are looking at real geometry.

CheckMate Pro certification covers scale and topology, which for a case that is always shown next to a hand or a shelf is the difference between a period prop and a slightly wrong one. Artwork drops onto the front insert as a texture, so branding a case for a music or software mock-up takes one map.

Seven versions sit on this page: single and double cases, clear, blue, black and green trays, an open case and a flipping-tray double. That covers most of what a shelf full of discs actually looks like. Sold 170 times since 2021, into retro interiors, music packaging and period set dressing.

A discarded newspaper, crumpled and half-open the way one actually lies on a pavement. 39,588 polygons in quads only go into the folds, because a flat plane with a paper texture reads as a poster, not as litter, the moment a light rakes across it.

Four maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the print, the creases and the grime. Non-overlapping UVs mean you can drop your own front page onto it, which is how this model usually gets used: a dated headline in a street scene does more for a period than most set dressing.

It is built to CheckMate specification rather than certified, so the topology and scale follow the same rules without the third-party review stamp. Sold 166 times since 2016, into street scenes, post-apocalyptic environments and film set dressing.

An onshore wind turbine at 20,879 polygons, which is light enough to plant a hundred of them across a ridge and still move the viewport. The nacelle, hub and blade twist are correct, so the silhouette reads right at the distance turbines are usually seen from.

The texture work is unusually generous for a model this light: 18 maps at 6144 x 6144 and 4096 x 4096, which means the tower holds up when the camera does come close to the base. CheckMate Pro certification and real-world scale keep it honest next to buildings and vehicles, where a turbine that is even slightly the wrong height looks like a toy.

It carries no manufacturer branding, so there is nothing to clear before it appears in an energy company presentation. Sold 165 times since 2016, into renewable energy visualisation, landscape work and infrastructure animation.

A cab-over delivery truck at 330,548 polygons: the flat nose, the high cab and the box body that makes up most of urban freight traffic. The detail sits where it earns its keep, on the cab face, the mirrors, the roller door and the wheels, because those are what a viewer tracks when the truck moves through frame.

Fourteen maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover paint, glass, rubber and the aluminium box. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology, so it parks correctly against a loading dock without anyone measuring.

Eight versions share the page: rigged builds for animation, simple-interior builds for background traffic, white cargo variants and fully generic bodies for commercial work. The Isuzu-badged versions carry editorial terms; the generic ones do not. Sold 164 times since 2017, into city scenes, logistics visualisation and simulation.

An empty Santa sleigh at 30,002 polygons, with the scrollwork on the sides, the runners and the bench seat modelled rather than implied. Empty is the useful part: you fill it with your own sacks, parcels and props instead of fighting a fixed pile of gifts that never matches the client's product.

Twenty-four maps at 2048 x 2048 and 1024 x 1024 cover the painted wood, the gold trim and the upholstery. CheckMate Pro certification means it arrives at real-world scale, which matters when the sleigh has to seat a character rather than just sit in the background of a card.
A second version with fur trim shares the page for softer, more traditional Christmas work. Sold 164 times since 2019, into holiday advertising, seasonal interiors and animation.

A set of cut diamonds supplied as a single product: the standard shapes a jewellery scene needs, built with correct facet counts rather than approximated cones, because a diamond is nothing but its facets and the light bouncing between them.

CheckMate Pro certification covers real-world scale and clean topology, which is not a formality here: a stone modelled at the wrong size renders with the wrong dispersion and looks like glass. Material setup follows the same rules across every stone in the set, so a shader tweak on one carries to the rest.

Buying them together is the point. One product, a full tray of cuts, consistent topology and scale across all of them, which is what you want when a ring needs a centre stone plus a row of accents. Sold 161 times since 2017, into jewellery advertising, packaging and product visualisation.

A modular scaffold bay at 207,920 polygons in quads only, built the way real scaffolding goes together: standards, ledgers, braces, boards and toe rails as separate parts. That is what lets you clone a bay along a facade and have the joints line up instead of ending with a lattice that reads as wallpaper.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 carry the galvanised steel, the scuffed planks and the paint marks that keep a construction set from looking new. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which is essential for a system that has to match the storey height of the building behind it.

A second construction scaffolding version sits on the same page for different frame proportions. Sold 156 times since 2015, into architectural visualisation, renovation presentations and film set builds.

A mirror ball built as actual tiles: 29,188 polygons in quads only, each facet a separate plane rather than a sphere with a reflective texture. That distinction is the entire model. Real tiles throw real light dots across a room, and no shader trick reproduces the way those dots stretch and slide when the ball turns.

Three maps at 4096 x 4096 cover the mirrored glass and the slight tarnish along the seams. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which matters for a prop whose job is to be hung from a ceiling at a believable height and to cast a pattern sized to the room.

Three versions share the page, including a rainbow-tinted ball for scenes that need colour in the reflections rather than plain silver. Sold 155 times since 2015, into club and party interiors, music video work and event visualisation.

A theatre curtain at 229,816 polygons, and the polygons are all in the folds. Draped fabric is one of the few things that cannot be faked with a normal map: the eye tracks the silhouette where the cloth leaves the rail, and a flat plane gives itself away instantly under a stage light.

Five maps carry the material, with the main ones authored at 8192 x 8192 and support maps at 2048 x 2048. That resolution is deliberate: velvet lives or dies on the fine sheen across the nap, and at 4K a full-height curtain across a frame starts to blur. CheckMate Pro certification covers scale and topology.
Sold 153 times since 2019, into theatre and opera sets, award-show presentations, product reveals and any shot that needs a red velvet frame for something else.

1,200 polygons in quads only, and that is all a soap bubble should ever cost. The whole effect lives in the material: a thin-film sheen that shifts colour across the surface and a rim that goes almost invisible where the sphere turns away from camera.

A single 2048 x 2048 map drives that film, and StemCell certification means the PBR setup is standardised, so the iridescence survives the trip into a game engine instead of collapsing into a grey ball. Scatter a few dozen at different scales and you have a bath, a summer garden or a detergent commercial.

A second soapy variant shares the page for a slightly different film pattern. At $9 it is a low-risk building block, and it has sold 151 times since 2018, into advertising, children's content and motion graphics.

A 12-inch record at 9,412 polygons in quads only, with the groove band, the run-out and the raised label edge in the mesh. Eight maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 do the rest, and that resolution is what lets a close-up show the concentric groove lines instead of a smooth black disc.

The label is its own texture area, so putting your own artwork on the record is a single map swap. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which is the difference between a record that sits correctly on a turntable and one that has to be scaled by eye every time.

Six versions live on this page: plain records plus Beatles, Bob Marley and Elvis Presley sleeves and labels for period set dressing. The named ones carry editorial terms; the plain record does not, which is the one for commercial work. Sold 150 times since 2015.

A soft-serve swirl in a waffle cone at 25,866 polygons, with the swirl modelled turn by turn and the waffle grid cut into the geometry rather than bump-mapped. Food work punishes shortcuts: a printed waffle pattern flattens under a rim light, and the swirl edge is where the eye lands first.

Ten maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the cream surface, the baked cone and the crumb. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so the cone is the size of something a hand can hold, which is exactly the check a food client makes first.
Three versions sit on the page: this one, a strawberry swirl in a pink waffle cone, and a vanilla scoop version. Sold 147 times since 2019, into food advertising, packaging design and summer scenes.

A claw machine at 203,824 polygons, supplied empty on purpose. The cabinet, the glass, the gantry, the claw and the prize chute are all there; what is not there is a fixed pile of plush toys, which means you fill it with whatever the scene needs instead of working around someone else's prizes.

Ten maps at 2048 x 2048 cover the painted steel, the decals and the scuffed acrylic. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology, which matters for an arcade cabinet that has to stand next to characters at a believable height.
A rigged version shares the page for anyone who needs the claw to travel and drop on camera. Sold 147 times since 2018, into arcade and mall interiors, games and film set dressing.

A tractor unit and box trailer at 724,720 polygons, which is the heaviest thing most road scenes will carry and worth it: a semi is enormous in frame, and the fifth wheel, the air lines, the mudflaps and the trailer ribs are all inspected by the eye whether the viewer knows it or not. The interior is simplified, which is the right call behind tinted glass.

Sixteen maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover paint, chrome, rubber and the aluminium trailer skin. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so it fits a loading bay and a lane width without adjustment.

Three versions share the page: a rigged build for animation and a fully detailed generic body alongside this one. No manufacturer badging, so nothing to clear before it appears in commercial work. Sold 144 times since 2020, into logistics visualisation, highway scenes and simulation.

A rosemary sprig at 32,128 polygons in quads only, with every needle built as geometry. That sounds extravagant for a herb until the camera is a hand's width from a plated dish, which is where food photography usually lives, and card-based needles fall apart the moment they catch a highlight.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the waxy needle surface, the pale underside and the woody stem. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so the sprig is the size of one you would actually lay on a roast rather than a decorative branch.
Sold 144 times since 2018, into food advertising, packaging design and restaurant interiors, where a single correct herb does more for a plate than any amount of post work.

A classic acetate frame at 7,990 polygons, with the hinges, the nose pads and the lens bevel modelled. Eyewear is a close-up product: the join where the arm meets the frame is the first place a viewer decides whether a render is a photograph or not.

Nine maps at 2048 x 2048 cover the frame, the metal detail and the gradient tint, which is the point of this version - the lens shades from light blue at the top to near clear at the bottom, the way a real gradient lens behaves. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so it fits a face rig without guessing.
Four versions share the page: two gold aviators including a leather-trim build, and a plain classic frame. Sold 143 times since 2017, into eyewear advertising, fashion lookbooks and character work.

A helium balloon and its ribbon at 5,166 polygons, which is as light as this prop should be, because balloons are never used one at a time. The neck pinch, the slight pear shape under buoyancy and the curl of the ribbon are all in the mesh, so a bunch of them reads correctly without any per-instance work.

A single 2048 x 2048 map carries the latex, including the subtle translucency that stops a balloon from looking like a painted ball when light passes through it. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology.
Sold 142 times since 2018, into party and event scenes, advertising, children's content and motion graphics where a balloon is doing the emotional work of the frame.

A set of prescription bottles at 35,384 polygons total, with the child-resistant cap threads, the shoulder radius and the label panel built properly. Pharmacy props are label-driven: everything a viewer reads is on a flat face, and that face has to be clean geometry with room for text.

Two maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the amber plastic and the label stock. Non-overlapping UVs mean you can drop a client's own label artwork onto each bottle without unwrapping anything. CheckMate Pro certification covers real-world scale, which is the detail a pharmaceutical client checks first.

Buying the set matters here: the sizes relate to each other correctly, so a shelf or a counter arrangement looks like a real dispensary rather than one bottle scaled three ways. Sold 141 times since 2019, into medical visualisation, pharmacy interiors and healthcare presentation.

A hibiscus in full bloom at 17,885 polygons, with the five petals, the long staminal column and the leaves built to hold their shape at close range. Hibiscus is a flower people know: the column sticking out past the petals is the detail that makes it read as hibiscus rather than as a generic red bloom.

Six maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the petal veining and the translucency that makes the colour glow when light comes from behind. StemCell certification means standardised PBR materials, so it behaves the same in a real-time engine as in an offline render.
Three versions share the page: this red bloom, an orange one and a pink one. Pick the colour the set needs. Sold 139 times since 2020, into tropical interiors, cosmetics and resort visualisation.

A supermarket trolley at 13,184 polygons, with the wire basket built as actual wire. That is the whole trick: a trolley is mostly empty space, and the crossing pattern of the mesh is what sells it, so faking the basket with a transparency card falls apart the second anything casts a shadow through it.

Two maps at 2048 x 2048 cover the chromed steel and the plastic handle. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which matters for a prop that has to fit an aisle and stand at the right height next to a shopper.
Sold 139 times since 2017, into retail interiors, supermarket visualisation and advertising. It is unbranded, so there is nothing to clear before it appears in a commercial scene.

A fedora at 9,100 polygons in quads only, with the pinch crown, the centre dent and the snapped brim built into the mesh. Those three shapes are the hat: get the pinch wrong and it reads as a trilby or a costume-shop approximation, which is exactly what a period shot cannot afford.

Four maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the felt nap and the grosgrain band. Felt is directional, and that is where the resolution goes. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so it sits on a head rig without a scale hunt.

Ten versions share the page: brown, blue, black and royal blue bodies, a second crown shape in two colours, and gentleman and classic men's variants. Same block, different felt. Sold 137 times since 2015, into character work, period film and fashion visualisation.

324,811 polygons for a crown, and every one of them is doing something. The arches, the cross pattee, the orb, the jewel settings and the pearls on the cross bands are individual pieces of geometry, because a coronation crown is a jewellery object at architectural scale: the camera always comes close enough to count stones.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover the gold, the enamel and the velvet cap. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so the crown is sized to a human head rather than to a monument, which is a mistake that is surprisingly easy to make with regalia.
Three versions share the page, including one with the ermine fur band modelled. Sold 134 times since 2015, into historical documentary work, film, games and editorial illustration.

A gas barbecue at 46,871 polygons in quads only, with the lid, the cooking grates, the side shelves, the control knobs and the wheels built as separate parts. Grates are the reason to buy a modelled grill rather than fake one: they carry the shadow pattern that everything on the grill sits in.

Five maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover the stainless steel, the enamelled lid and the cast iron. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so it stands at counter height next to a patio set instead of looming.
Sold 132 times since 2015, into exterior architectural visualisation, outdoor living scenes and appliance advertising. Unbranded, so no clearance is needed before it appears in commercial work.

3,960,288 polygons and 4,086,746 vertices, which makes this one of the heaviest assets in the catalogue and tells you what it is for: hero shots of a high-speed train where the camera travels along the body and every window frame, roof fairing, bogie and pantograph has to be there.

Thirty maps at 4096 x 4096 cover the livery, the glass, the underframe and the wear along the skirt. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology across all of that geometry, which at this size is the difference between an asset that opens and one that fights your scene.

A second version of the ICE 4 intercity build shares the page. Sold 129 times since 2015, into transport visualisation, infrastructure film work and simulation. Editorial terms apply, so it belongs in documentary, film and simulation rather than brand advertising.

A belt conveyor section at 40,890 polygons, built as a module: frame, rollers, belt, legs and side guides as separate parts so you can chain sections into a line as long as the factory needs instead of stretching one mesh until the rollers smear.

Six maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 carry the painted frame, the rubber belt and the worn metal at the contact points. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which is what keeps boxes, bottles or parcels sitting on the belt at a believable height when they arrive from another asset.
A second belt conveyor version shares the page for a different frame profile. Sold 128 times since 2015, into industrial and logistics visualisation, factory animation and process explainers.

A fifth-generation stealth fighter at 206,388 polygons, with the faceted intakes, the sawtooth panel joins, the weapons bay doors and the lift-fan hatch all modelled. Those edges are the aircraft: stealth shaping is what the silhouette is made of, and rounding it off turns the jet into a generic fighter.

Nine maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 carry the low-visibility grey, the panel lines and the radar-absorbent surface variation that keeps the skin from reading as flat paint. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology.

Nine versions share the page, and they cover the ways this jet actually gets used: rigged builds for flight animation, builds with a pilot in the cockpit, an OK-gesture pose for canopy-open ground shots, and dedicated Maya rigs. Sold 123 times since 2017, into defence visualisation, simulation and film.

A breakaway rim and backboard mount at 49,529 polygons, with the spring hinge, the net hooks and the bracket bolts modelled. The net is where a rim model usually fails: this one has the cord built as geometry, so it hangs and catches light instead of reading as a printed cone.

Nine maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover the powder-coated orange, the padded backboard edge and the nylon net. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which is not negotiable for sports equipment - a rim at the wrong diameter is visible the moment a ball approaches it.
A generic rim version shares the page for work that cannot carry brand marks. Sold 123 times since 2015, into sports broadcast graphics, arena visualisation and games.

A ring of water caught mid-air at 21,180 polygons: the sheet, the rim and the droplets breaking off it, modelled rather than simulated. That is the whole argument for this asset. A fluid solve for one hero splash costs a day of machine time and still needs art direction; this one opens, lights and renders in an afternoon.

The texture is a single map at 8192 x 8192, which is unusually large for a prop this light and entirely justified: water is refraction and thin highlights, and those are the first things to break up at lower resolution. StemCell certification means the PBR setup is standardised across renderers.

An orange version shares the page for juice and soft-drink work, where the same shape has to read as fruit liquid rather than water. Sold 123 times since 2017, into beverage advertising, cosmetics and motion graphics.

The crown is what a drop makes when it lands: a circular wall of liquid with beads forming along the top edge. This one is 24,884 polygons, with those beads as geometry, because they are the detail that identifies the shape and they fall apart as soon as anyone tries to fake them with a bump map.

One map at 8192 x 8192 carries the surface. StemCell certification standardises the PBR materials, so the same crown reads correctly whether it is lit by an HDRI in a product render or by a game engine's sky.

Four versions sit on the page, and they are the four liquids this shape is actually bought for: water, milk, chocolate and orange. Same physics, different viscosity in the material, which is why they belong together rather than on four competing pages. Sold 121 times since 2017, into dairy, confectionery and beverage advertising.

The A7L is the suit from the Moon landings and the Skylab missions, and it is a documented object: the cover layer seams, the pressure connectors on the chest, the lunar boots and the visor assembly are all matters of record. This build holds them at 25,662 polygons, which keeps it usable in a scene rather than only in a hero still.

Seven maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the beta cloth weave, the aluminised visor and the wear that a suit picks up in use. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which matters for a suit that has to fit a human figure and stand next to a lander at the right height.

Sold 120 times since 2016, into space documentary work, museum and educational visualisation, games and film. Historical accuracy is the selling point here, and it is the reason this one keeps moving nine years after release.

A 2 iron at 2,274 polygons, which is about as economical as a golf club gets while keeping the loft angle, the hosel bend and the grooved face correct. Those three things are what a golfer looks at, and they are also what a swing animation needs in order to make contact convincingly.

A second watermelon slice version shares the page for a different cut. Sold 92 times since 2017, into food advertising, summer scenes, packaging design and restaurant visualisation.

A set of vallisneria for the back wall of an aquarium, at 15,432 polygons. These are ribbon plants: long twisted blades that rise from a base and bend under the water's motion, and the twist has to be in the geometry because it is what distinguishes vallisneria from every other green aquarium plant.

Two maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the blade surfaces including the translucency that underwater plants show when lit from above. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which keeps the plants in proportion to the fish and the tank.

It is supplied as a set rather than a single plant, which is how aquarium planting actually works: a background row is several clumps at different heights. A spiral vallisneria version shares the page. Sold 92 times since 2018, into aquarium and aquascaping visualisation, pet retail and nature work.

3,111,707 polygons across a diesel locomotive and a covered hopper car. That is hero-shot territory: the walkway grating, the radiator grilles, the truck side frames, the brake rigging and the hopper hatches are all built, which is what a camera travelling along a train demands.

Twenty-nine maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the livery, the reflective stripes and the rust and brake dust that make freight equipment look worked rather than new. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale and clean topology at this size, which is not trivial.

Six versions share the page: CSX and Norfolk Southern liveries, ES44AC builds, and a generic diesel electric locomotive with freight cars for work that cannot carry a railroad's marks. Sold 91 times since 2015, into rail simulation, film, documentary and industrial visualisation.

The plumeria range supplied as one product: the bloom in its colour variants and the arrangements built from them, so a lei, a table scatter or a tropical planting can be assembled from a single purchase instead of five.

CheckMate Pro certification covers scale, topology and material naming across the set, which is what makes a collection worth more than the sum of its flowers. Consistent scale means blooms from different variants sit together correctly in the same arrangement.

Sold 90 times since 2017, into resort and spa visualisation, cosmetics and fragrance work, and tropical interiors. Buying the collection is the sensible route when a scene needs plumeria in more than one colour.

A pair of pleated curtains at 168,766 polygons. Drapery is one of the few interior elements where polygon count directly buys realism: the fold spacing, the way the fabric gathers at the heading and the soft break at the floor are all silhouette, and silhouette cannot be faked by a normal map.

Six maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the weave and the subtle sheen that separates a lined curtain from a bedsheet. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so the drop matches standard ceiling heights and the curtains do not float above the floor.

Five versions share the page in grey, green, brown and yellow, plus a classic set with tiebacks on a rod. Sold 89 times since 2015, into interior visualisation, real estate presentation and film set dressing.

An emoji hand at 1,376 polygons, built in the simplified, rounded style that emoji actually use rather than as a realistic hand shrunk down. That distinction is the product: an anatomically correct hand in a flat-coloured emoji set looks wrong immediately.

Five maps at 1024 x 1024 cover the flat colour and the soft shading. StemCell certification means standardised PBR materials, so the whole set behaves identically in a real-time engine, which is where emoji usually end up - in motion graphics, UI animation and social content.

Eighteen versions share the page, and that is the real value here: handshake, raised hand, raised back of hand, palms up together, OK hand, the Vulcan salute, pointing gestures and more. A full gesture vocabulary from one product. Sold 88 times since 2020.

977,700 polygons for a hay bale, and it is not excessive. A bale is a compressed mass of individual stalks, and the ends are where you see them all in cross-section: modelled straws are the only way that face reads correctly, and it is nearly always the face pointed at camera.

Two maps at 2048 x 2048 carry the straw colour variation and the twine. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which matters when bales are stacked in a barn or loaded on a trailer and the stack height has to make sense.
A square straw bale version shares the page for different farm work. Sold 88 times since 2015, into agricultural visualisation, rural exteriors, film set dressing and games.

A folded paper boat at 1,803 polygons, with the creases built as real edges. Origami is all crease: the sharp folds and the slight spring where the paper resists being flattened are the only things that separate a paper boat from a plastic toy, and they have to be geometry.

Two maps at 2048 x 2048 carry the paper stock. Non-overlapping UVs mean you can print anything onto the sheet the boat is folded from, which is where the newspaper version on the same page comes from.

Sold 88 times since 2018, into advertising and motion graphics, childhood and nostalgia themes, and conceptual work where a small fragile object has to carry a metaphor. Paper boats do a lot of symbolic work for a $19 asset.

A Viking-era arrow at 632 polygons in quads only: the shaft, the forged head and the bound fletching. At this weight you can fill a quiver, load a volley or stick two dozen into a shield wall without a second thought, which is exactly how arrows get used.

Five maps carry it, authored at 2816 x 384 - a long, narrow texture shape that matches the object instead of wasting most of a square map on empty space. That is a small piece of craft that pays off across a hundred instances. CheckMate Pro certification covers scale and topology.
Sold 88 times since 2019, into historical film and documentary work, games, museum and educational visualisation. Period-correct fletching and head shape are why it gets picked over a generic arrow.

A rail tank car at 538,713 polygons, with the dome, the walkways, the ladders, the handrails, the brake gear and the truck assemblies modelled. Tank cars are defined by their fittings: the barrel is simple, and everything that says rolling stock is bolted to the outside of it.

Eight maps at 4096 x 4096 carry the painted steel, the placards and the streaking that a tank car picks up in service. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which is what lets a consist be assembled from this and other cars without a height mismatch.

Six versions share the page, covering several tank car bodies and profiles, so a train can be made up of varied cars rather than one model repeated. Sold 87 times since 2015, into rail simulation, industrial visualisation and film.

A perfume bottle at 7,127 polygons, and the geometry is doing something specific: thick faceted glass with a stopper, built so that refraction has something real to bend through. A bottle modelled as a thin shell renders like a plastic prop no matter how good the shader is.

Six maps at 4096 x 4096 cover the glass, the label and the cap. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, which for fragrance is not cosmetic: the perceived size of a bottle is part of how the product is read, and a bottle rendered larger than life looks cheap.

Six versions share the page, including generic perfume bottles, a cosmetic spray bottle and a classic women's eau de parfum. The branded ones carry editorial terms; the generic bottles are the ones for commercial work. Sold 87 times since 2017, into fragrance and cosmetics visualisation.
